opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it changes things at a pretty fundamental level, because right now there's a deep mismatch between the algorithms we care about and the hardware we run them on.

Almost all of modern machine learning is, at its core, probabilistic. We're learning distributions, sampling from them, reasoning under uncertainty. But we run all of it on digital hardware designed to be as deterministic as possible. We spend enormous amounts of energy fighting the noise in transistors, forcing everything into clean ones and zeros, and then we spend more energy using pseudorandom number generators to simulate randomness on top of that deterministic substrate. From a physics standpoint, that's wasteful. Nature is already noisy and stochastic, so why not harness that noise as a computational resource instead of suppressing it?

That's the bet behind probabilistic or thermodynamic computing: build hardware whose natural physical dynamics *are* the sampling process. If the hardware natively relaxes toward samples from some distribution you've programmed, like an energy-based model, then sampling becomes nearly free in terms of energy and time, rather than being the expensive bottleneck it is today.

That changes what kinds of models win. A lot of the current landscape is shaped by what GPUs are good at: big dense matrix multiplies and backprop through deterministic feedforward networks. That's partly why transformers took over. They map beautifully onto the hardware. It's a sort of hardware lottery. Energy-based models, Boltzmann machines, more general probabilistic graphical models: these were always elegant and expressive, but they lost out largely because sampling from them on digital hardware is painfully slow. Probabilistic hardware flips that cost structure. Suddenly the models that are most natural for representing uncertainty and complex multimodal distributions become the cheap ones.

So I'd expect a few things. First, a resurgence of energy-based and generative models that are explicitly probabilistic, potentially with much better energy efficiency per sample than diffusion models on GPUs. Second, hybrid systems where digital accelerators handle certain parts and probabilistic cores handle the sampling-heavy parts, the way we already pair CPUs with GPUs. Third, and more speculatively, models that are much better at reasoning under uncertainty, exploration, and hedging rather than giving confident point estimates.

And zooming out, energy is becoming the real constraint on AI scaling. If we want intelligence to scale with civilization's energy budget, we need to get far more intelligence per joule. Making the hardware match the physics of the problem is, I think, one of the biggest levers we have left.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers took over partly because they map beautifully onto GPUs, calling it a “hardware lottery,” which frames their success as dependent on hardware fit.

r002.rationale: It says probabilistic hardware “flips that cost structure” and changes which models are cheap, explicitly describing a shift in the algorithmic fitness landscape.

r003.rationale: The response predicts a resurgence of probabilistic models, but does not say an abrupt hardware-driven shift will cause an explosion of exploration of new algorithmic designs.

r004.rationale: It characterizes modern machine learning as probabilistic, but does not observe that incumbent algorithms are converging toward more probabilistic approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the short answer is that probabilistic hardware changes what's cheap, and in machine learning what's cheap is what gets scaled, and what gets scaled is what wins. Right now the thing that's cheap is deterministic matrix multiplication, so we build models that are essentially giant deterministic functions, and we bolt randomness on afterwards as an afterthought. You sample from a softmax at the very end, or you inject Gaussian noise in a diffusion model, and you spend an enormous number of flops pretending to be random using circuits that are engineered at great expense to never be random. If you look at the energy budget of a modern accelerator, a surprising amount of it is spent fighting thermal noise so that every bit lands exactly where it should. That's a strange thing to do if the algorithm you're running wants noise anyway.

What probabilistic hardware does is flip that around. You build a substrate where the fundamental primitive is sampling from a distribution rather than evaluating a deterministic function. The physics gives you the randomness for free, because the transistors or the magnetic tunnel junctions or whatever the device is are operating right at the edge where thermal fluctuations are the signal rather than the enemy. And the moment sampling becomes as cheap as a multiply-accumulate is today, a whole class of algorithms that we abandoned for engineering reasons rather than for scientific reasons becomes viable again.

I'd point to energy-based models as the obvious example. Boltzmann machines, Hopfield-style networks, all of the stuff that was the mainstream in the eighties and nineties and then got buried by backprop on GPUs. Those models didn't lose because they're bad models of the world. They lost because training them requires you to draw samples from an equilibrium distribution, and doing that with Markov chain Monte Carlo on a deterministic chip is horrendously slow. If instead you have a physical system that just relaxes to its Boltzmann distribution because that's what thermodynamics does, then the hard part of the algorithm is literally the thing the hardware wants to do anyway. You're no longer simulating physics, you're using physics.

So concretely I'd expect a few things to happen in the model landscape. First, generative modelling becomes native rather than iterative. Diffusion models today take hundreds or thousands of sequential denoising steps, and each step is a full deterministic forward pass. On a sampling-native substrate you can collapse a lot of that into the dynamics of the device. Second, I think you'll see a return of models that reason with uncertainty from the ground up, where the weights themselves are distributions and inference is sampling over them. Bayesian deep learning has been this perpetual bridesmaid because it's about ten times more expensive than the point-estimate alternative, and that cost differential goes away if your hardware is probabilistic by construction. Third, and this is the one I'm most excited about, I think the training procedure itself changes. Backprop is a very particular algorithm that happens to map beautifully onto deterministic parallel hardware. It's not obvious that it maps well onto a stochastic physical system, and the alternatives, things like contrastive learning on energy-based models or equilibrium propagation, are much more local and much more like what you'd want to do if you were trying to train something that behaves like a physical system rather than a spreadsheet.

The way I'd frame the long arc is that we're coming out of a brief historical window where digital computing was so good and so cheap that it made sense to simulate everything, including randomness, on top of it. Nature doesn't do that. The brain runs at about twenty watts and is noisy as hell, and it's noisy by design, not by failure. I think the trajectory of machine learning over the next decade is going to look like a reconvergence with that fact. Not because of some romantic appeal to biology, but because the energy wall is real, the von Neumann bottleneck is real, and the algorithms that scale best in that regime are going to be the ones that stop fighting the physics and start using it.

And to be honest, the thing that will surprise people is that the models that come out of this probably won't look like today's transformers with a stochastic chip underneath. The hardware constraint shapes the architecture. GPUs gave us dense matmuls and therefore attention. A substrate where sampling is free will give us something else, and I don't think anyone can say exactly what yet. That's the part that makes it interesting.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GPUs enabled dense matrix multiplication and therefore attention, and predicts that a sampling-native substrate will produce different architectures.

r002.rationale: It explains that making sampling cheap changes which algorithms are practical and therefore changes the model landscape.

r003.rationale: The candidate anticipates new designs but does not clearly say an abrupt hardware shift will trigger an explosion of exploration.

r004.rationale: It predicts a move toward probabilistic models, but does not say incumbent algorithms are already converging toward probabilistic approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is that randomness can become a computational resource rather than something we have to simulate. We tend to think of a model as a mathematical object that we then map onto hardware, but the hardware also shapes which models are practical. If sampling becomes cheap, that changes the kinds of models we’re willing to build.

For example, you might put more emphasis on energy-based models, where you learn a landscape and inference involves exploring that landscape, rather than doing a fixed sequence of deterministic operations. You could also make uncertainty a more integral part of computation, instead of something you estimate by running a model many times.

But there’s a crucial distinction between getting random bits cheaply and getting useful samples cheaply. You still have to encode the distribution you care about, and the system has to explore it effectively. If it gets stuck, the fact that the underlying physics is stochastic doesn’t solve your problem.

So I’d expect a co-evolution of models, training algorithms, and hardware. The opportunity is to find architectures where the natural dynamics of the device do a substantial part of the computation for you. That could open up a different set of trade-offs in efficiency and expressiveness, rather than simply making today’s models run faster.

r001.rationale: It says hardware shapes which models are practical, but does not discuss transformers or present their success as contingent on hardware fit.

r002.rationale: It explains that hardware shapes which models are practical and that cheaper sampling could change the kinds of models people build.

r003.rationale: It mentions opening a different set of trade-offs, but not an abrupt landscape shift triggering an explosion of exploration.

r004.rationale: It discusses probabilistic computation and uncertainty, but does not say incumbent algorithms are already converging toward probabilistic approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes which models are economical to run, and that can change which models we choose to build. If your hardware is very good at deterministic matrix multiplication, you naturally build around that. If it can produce and manipulate randomness efficiently, then sampling can become a basic computational operation rather than an expensive extra step.

That could make probabilistic models more practical—models where you maintain a distribution over possible explanations or predictions instead of committing to a single answer. You might spend more computation exploring alternatives when a problem is ambiguous, and less when the answer is clear.

But there’s a co-design problem here. A source of random bits alone doesn’t give you useful inference. You need algorithms that turn the hardware’s particular dynamics into samples from the distribution you actually care about, and you need to account for the cost of moving data and controlling the device.

So I’d expect an evolution through hybrid systems. Deterministic computation handles the parts it does well, and probabilistic hardware handles sampling or search where it offers an advantage. If that advantage holds at the system level, model architectures will start adapting around it.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware influences which models are economical and built, but does not discuss transformers or frame their success as contingent on hardware fit.

r002.rationale: It explains that hardware changes which models are economical to run and therefore which models developers choose to build, describing a change in the landscape of algorithmic fitness.

r003.rationale: It predicts model architectures may adapt if probabilistic hardware offers a system-level advantage, but does not describe an abrupt shift or an explosion of exploration.

r004.rationale: It discusses probabilistic models becoming more practical, but does not say incumbent algorithms are already converging toward probabilistic approaches.
